circulose.types: CIRCULOSE itself is a dissolving pulp in sheet form, made from cotton-rich textile waste; it becomes a fiber only in a partner's viscose or lyocell plant. Fiber products made with it have been sold as CIRCULOSE viscose with about 30% or 50% recycled pulp content and CIRCULOSE lyocell with about 30%, the remainder being wood pulp, according to the producer. In 2025 Circulose announced a partnership with Jilin Chemical Fiber for viscose filament yarn and, later, a partner-only supply model in which pulp goes to brands with direct partnerships. Specifications such as viscosity and alpha-cellulose content matter to fiber makers; for shoppers the key figure is the recycled share.
circulose.fabrics: Fibers containing CIRCULOSE pulp go into the usual viscose and lyocell products, such as dresses, blouses, knit tops and denim blends, and the Jilin partnership targets viscose filament yarn for smooth wovens. The producer reports that more than 250 styles have been made with brands including H&M, Levi's, Tommy Hilfiger, COS, Zara and Calvin Klein, and has since announced partnerships with EILEEN FISHER, Marimekko, Samsoe Samsoe and King Louie. Because the pulp is mixed with wood pulp and the resulting fiber is often blended with cotton or elastane, garments usually contain a minority of recycled cellulose.
circulose.quality: The garment label will list viscose, lyocell or rayon, never CIRCULOSE as a fiber. Ask the brand for two numbers: the recycled pulp share in the fiber and the fiber's share in the garment. Circulose announced in 2025 that it would trace material from pulp to finished apparel through TextileGenesis, a digital system that issues a token for each kilogram of pulp to prevent double counting, so brands can request that record. Fabric quality follows the fiber type: viscose from recycled pulp should be judged like any viscose for drape, seam strength and shrinkage.
pros: It makes dissolving pulp from discarded cotton garments, not only from production scraps.
Downstream fiber makers can use it in existing viscose and lyocell lines without new equipment.
Digital traceability through a token system is designed to stop the same recycled pulp being claimed twice.
It reduces the wood pulp needed for the share it replaces.
cons: The original company, Renewcell, went bankrupt in 2024, and supply has depended on restarting the plant.
Recycled share in fibers is typically 30 to 50%, and lower again in blended garments.
A partner-only model limits who can buy it and how widely it is available.
Independent life-cycle data are limited; most figures come from the producer.
circulose.impact: Circulose presents its pulp as replacing wood pulp and diverting cotton waste; the balance depends on energy use, bleaching chemistry and yields at Ortviken, and on the viscose or lyocell plant that later dissolves the pulp. The fiber stage carries the usual impacts of viscose, including carbon disulfide handling, or of lyocell. No independent peer-reviewed life-cycle study specific to CIRCULOSE was found for this entry. At end of life, regenerated cellulose behaves better than polyester in one respect: a 2019 study (Zambrano and colleagues) found rayon microfibers biodegraded in aerobic aquatic tests while polyester microfibers persisted. The commercial history matters to impact too: a plant that sits idle for lack of orders diverts no waste.
circulose.care: Care follows the fiber made from the pulp. For viscose garments: wash cold to 30 C on a delicate cycle, do not wring, dry flat or hanging, and iron on medium (about 150 C) on the reverse while slightly damp. For lyocell: wash at 30 to 40 C, gentle cycle, inside out, avoid overloading to limit fibrillation. Avoid chlorine bleach with both. Store dry to prevent mildew. Recycled pulp does not change care needs. When the garment is a blend with elastane or polyester, use the most heat-sensitive fiber's limits and follow the care label.
faq: No. It is a recycled dissolving pulp that fiber producers turn into viscose or lyocell. The garment label will show that generic fiber, and the brand may add that it contains CIRCULOSE pulp.
How much recycled material is in CIRCULOSE garments?

Fibers made with it have typically contained about 30% or 50% recycled pulp, with wood pulp making up the rest. If the garment also includes cotton or elastane, the overall recycled share is lower. Ask the brand for the exact figure.

Renewcell, which developed CIRCULOSE, was declared bankrupt in February 2024. The investment firm Altor bought the business and plant later that year and renamed it Circulose, which announced plans to restart production in the fourth quarter of 2026.
notable: Circulose's traceability partner issues a digital token for every kilogram of pulp to record each processing step and prevent double counting.
The producer reports that more than 250 garment styles have been made with CIRCULOSE across well-known fashion brands.
